title: 04. BM25 & Lexical Search: Language Model for IR — Query Likelihood
summary: The Language Model (LM) approach to IR treats each document as a probability distribution over words — a language model θ_D.

sections.title: ① Concept Explanation
sections.body:
The Language Model (LM) approach to IR treats each document as a probability distribution over words — a language model θ_D. The relevance of document D to query Q is measured as the probability of generating the query from the document's language model: P(Q | θ_D). The document that most likely "generated" the query is ranked first. Because maximum-likelihood estimation assigns zero probability to unseen terms (the zero-probability problem), smoothing is required — Dirichlet smoothing and Jelinek-Mercer smoothing are the standard approaches.

$$P(Q|\theta_D) = \prod_{t \in Q} P(t|\theta_D)$$

$$P(t|\theta_D)_{\text{Dirichlet}} = \frac{c(t,D) + \mu \cdot P(t|C)}{|D| + \mu}$$

where C is the collection language model and μ is the smoothing parameter (typically 1000–2000).

sections.title: ④ Visual Explanation
sections.body:
```
LANGUAGE MODEL FOR IR
══════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Document D1: "BM25 scoring uses term frequency"
  θ_D1: P("BM25"|D1)=0.15, P("scoring"|D1)=0.10, P("term"|D1)=0.10
  
  Query Q: "BM25 term"
  
  P(Q|θ_D1) = P("BM25"|D1) × P("term"|D1)
             = 0.15 × 0.10 = 0.015  ← high → relevant!
  
  Dirichlet Smoothing (μ=1000):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                  c(t,D) + μ·P(t|C)                     │
  │  P(t|θ_D) =  ─────────────────────                     │
  │                     |D| + μ                             │
  │                                                         │
  │  c(t,D)    = raw count of t in D                        │
  │  μ·P(t|C)  = pseudo-counts from collection              │
  │  |D| + μ   = effective document length + prior          │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  Effect of μ on document length:
  Short doc (|D|=50):  50/(50+1000) ≈ 5%  own LM, 95% collection
  Long  doc (|D|=5000): 5000/(5000+1000) ≈ 83% own LM, 17% collection
```

quiz.question: What is the zero-probability problem in query likelihood?
options: If posting lists have average length P, AND query processes O(N × P_min) comparisons where P_min is the length of the shortest list.
New York" ≠ {"New", "York"} semantically. BoW matches documents with "New" and "York" anywhere, not necessarily adjacent.
The collection is pre-indexed; only the query varies.
If any query term t doesn't appear in document D, then P(t|D)=0, making P(Q|D)=0 regardless of how relevant D is.
quiz.explanation: If any query term t doesn't appear in document D, then P(t|D)=0, making P(Q|D)=0 regardless of how relevant D is. Smoothing blends the document LM with a background collection LM.

quiz.question: What does Dirichlet smoothing model intuitively?
options: The collection is pre-indexed; only the query varies.
Instead of P(Q|D), score documents by -KL(θ_Q || θ_D) — the KL divergence from the query LM to the document LM.
(1) No relevance info → use RSJ with uniform priors. (2) After user interaction, collect R relevant docs → re-estimate P(t|R=1).
A document "borrows" μ pseudo-counts from the collection distribution.
quiz.explanation: A document "borrows" μ pseudo-counts from the collection distribution. Short documents borrow more (get pulled toward collection LM); long documents are dominated by their own statistics. μ controls the strength of this prior.

quiz.question: What is Jelinek-Mercer smoothing?
options: The collection is pre-indexed; only the query varies.
Either TF=0 (term doesn't appear in the document) or IDF=0 (term appears in every document and is thus useless for discrimination).
The query uses different words than the document. E.g., query = "heart attack", document = "myocardial infarction".
Linear interpolation: P(t|θ_D) = (1−λ)·P(t|D) + λ·P(t|C). λ ∈ [0,1] is a fixed mixing coefficient.
quiz.explanation: Linear interpolation: P(t|θ_D) = (1−λ)·P(t|D) + λ·P(t|C). λ ∈ [0,1] is a fixed mixing coefficient. Unlike Dirichlet, it's not document-length-aware (same λ for all documents).

quiz.question: How does the LM approach compare to BM25?
options: BM25 is a specific parametric instantiation of the Robertson-Spärck Jones framework with TF saturation and length normalisation added empirically to improve TREC…
Maximum likelihood over the entire corpus: P(t|C) = total_count(t) / total_tokens.
(1) Boolean model, (2) Vector Space Model (TF-IDF), (3) Probabilistic model (BM25, BIM), (4) Language Model (query likelihood), (5) Neural/Dense retrieval (bi-encoders).
With Dirichlet smoothing, the query-likelihood LM score approximates BM25 scoring.
quiz.explanation: With Dirichlet smoothing, the query-likelihood LM score approximates BM25 scoring. Both have a TF component and a length normalisation term. The key difference: BM25 is a discriminative heuristic; LM has a generative probabilistic interpretation.

quiz.question: What is the translation language model?
options: The collection is pre-indexed; only the query varies.
Either TF=0 (term doesn't appear in the document) or IDF=0 (term appears in every document and is thus useless for discrimination).
A retrieval model defines how to measure relevance between query and document.
An extension that models the probability of generating a query term from a document term via a translation probability P(t_q | t_d).
quiz.explanation: An extension that models the probability of generating a query term from a document term via a translation probability P(t_q | t_d). This captures vocabulary mismatch (synonyms) within the LM framework.
